issues.legal_issue: An uncorroborated extrajudicial confession made to a person without demonstrated influence or status may carry very little evidentiary weight.
material_facts: The accused allegedly confessed to an acquaintance, saying he had done so because the police were pursuing him and he wished to avoid harassment.
The recipient had no demonstrated influence with the police or status to protect the accused, and there was no other evidence corroborating the confession.
issues.conclusion: The confession was a very weak piece of evidence and was hardly of any consequence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated an extrajudicial confession as weak evidence in the circumstances, particularly where the recipient had no demonstrated ability to protect the accused and there was no corroboration. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a murder conviction based on circumstantial evidence and makes an uncorroborated extrajudicial confession to a person without demonstrated influence, the confession has little evidentiary weight.

issues.legal_issue: A speculative motive unsupported by evidence of discord does not establish a motive for the alleged offence.
material_facts: The alleged motive was that the deceased father intended to transfer land to the accused's son.
A will had been executed in the accused's favour, and there was no evidence of poor relations or a dispute between father and son.
issues.conclusion: The alleged motive was not established; the suggestion that the offence was committed to prevent a future change to the will was speculative.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the alleged motive against the evidence and found it speculative in the absence of evidence of discord. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.

issues.definition: When a property-based motive is alleged but an existing testamentary arrangement favors the accused and no family dispute is shown, the alleged motive is not established.

issues.legal_issue: Seeing an accused with the deceased on an earlier occasion does not establish a last-seen circumstance when the evidence does not exclude a plausible intervening account.
material_facts: A witness saw the accused with the deceased at a place of worship before the alleged murders.
The accused said that a relative had taken the deceased away on another pretext; the prosecution did not produce that relative or other evidence to rebut the account.
No other person connected with the deceased was called to establish that the deceased had not been seen after the earlier sighting.
issues.conclusion: The earlier sighting could not be treated as a circumstance of last seen against the accused.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the last-seen circumstance was not established where the prosecution did not negate the accused's account of an intervening departure and did not establish that the deceased were not seen thereafter. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.

predicates.accused_seen_with_deceased_earlier: A witness saw the accused with the deceased before the alleged offence.
predicates.plausible_intervening_account_unrebutted: The accused gave an account that another person took the deceased away, and the prosecution did not rebut it with evidence.
predicates.no_evidence_deceased_unseen_afterward: The prosecution did not establish that the deceased were not seen after the earlier sighting.

issues.definition: When an accused was seen with the deceased earlier but an intervening account remains unrebutted and there is no evidence the deceased were unseen afterward, the last-seen circumstance is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A discovery under section 27 of the Evidence Act is not an incriminating circumstance against an accused when knowledge of the place discovered cannot be attributed exclusively to that accused.
material_facts: The investigating officer had learned from another person that the bodies were buried in a field before recording the accused's disclosure.
The bodies were recovered from an open field surrounded by other fields, and the evidence did not show that only the accused could have known their location.
issues.conclusion: The recovery could not be treated as a circumstance against the accused under section 27 of the Evidence Act because exclusive knowledge could not be attributed to him.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 27 of the Evidence Act and held that, on these facts, a discovery was not a circumstance against the accused because the location was not shown to be within his exclusive knowledge. The judgment cites no earlier cases.

issues.legal_issue: Recovery of a deceased person's ordinary belongings from the place where the deceased lived does not, without more, support an inference against the accused.
material_facts: A tricycle and other belongings of the deceased were recovered from the small building where the deceased had lived.
The location was the deceased's residence, and the items' presence there was not otherwise significant.
issues.conclusion: No inference against the accused could be drawn from the recovery of those belongings.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no incriminating significance in finding the deceased's belongings where they were ordinarily kept. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.

predicates.belongings_expected_to_be_there: The belongings were ordinarily expected to be at that residence.

issues.definition: When the deceased's belongings are recovered from the place where they ordinarily lived and were expected to be, the recovery supports no inference against the accused.

issues.legal_issue: A murder conviction resting on circumstantial evidence cannot stand when the circumstances relied on do not prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The conviction rested on alleged motive, an earlier sighting of the accused with the deceased, an extrajudicial confession, recovery of the bodies, and recovery of the deceased's belongings.

The alleged motive was speculative, the earlier sighting did not establish a last-seen circumstance, the confession lacked corroboration, the open-field recovery did not show exclusive knowledge, and the belongings were found where the deceased had lived.
The bodies were recovered months after death in a disintegrated condition, and the prosecution did not call a relative to identify them.
issues.conclusion: The charge was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; the conviction and sentences were set aside and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court required the prosecution's circumstantial case to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt and concluded that the circumstances relied on did not do so. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this conclusion.
